data.text: Forms are where the control props pattern truly shines. Whether you're building a simple contact form or a complex multi-step signup flow, you need components that can work both as controlled inputs (managed by a form library like React Hook Form) and as standalone inputs (managing their own state). In this lesson, we'll build reusable form components that integrate seamlessly with React Hook Form and Zod validation, while maintaining full flexibility through control props.
Why Control Props Matter for Forms

items: Reusable form components can be used inside or outside a form library context
Controlled mode lets the form library own the state for validation and submission
Uncontrolled mode lets the component manage its own state for simpler or isolated use cases
The same component works in Storybook stories, unit tests, and production forms without modification

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Always accept a value/defaultValue pair in your reusable input components. This single convention makes every component work in both modes without extra configuration.

data.title: register vs Controller in React Hook Form

cards.title: register()
cards.description: Attaches a native HTML input to React Hook Form using refs. Best for simple inputs.
cons: Cannot be used with custom components

cards.title: Controller
cards.description: Wraps a controlled or custom component so it integrates with React Hook Form's state.

data.title: Create a Multi-Field Form
data.description: Using the dual-mode Input component and React Hook Form, build a form with email, password, and a custom toggle for newsletter subscription.
steps: Create a controlled Input component that accepts value/defaultValue
Set up useForm with a Zod schema for email and password validation
Use register() for the native inputs and Controller for the Toggle component
Implement error display with aria-live for accessibility
Add isSubmitting and isSubmitted states to the submit button
data.expectedOutcome: A fully functional, accessible form component that works in both controlled and uncontrolled modes.

items.question: When should I use Controller instead of register?
items.answer: Use Controller when your input is a custom component (like a date picker, select, or your own Toggle) that doesn't forward a ref to a native input. For standard inputs like text, email, and password, register() is simpler and more performant.

items.question: How does Zod provide type safety?
items.answer: Zod schemas are declared first, and you derive TypeScript types from them using z.infer<typeof schema>. This means your validation and types always stay in sync — no need to maintain separate interfaces.

items.question: Can I use the same Input component in Storybook and in a real form?
items.answer: Yes! Because the component supports both controlled and uncontrolled modes, you can render it in Storybook with defaultValue (no parent state needed) and in a real form with value/onChange wired to React Hook Form.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Control props let form components work with form libraries AND standalone
React Hook Form's register() is for native inputs; Controller is for custom components
Zod schemas provide both runtime validation and TypeScript types via z.infer
Always expose isSubmitting, isSubmitted, and errors to the user with accessible markup
The same dual-mode component can be used in Storybook, tests, and production
data.takeaway: Control props bridge the gap between reusable components and form libraries, giving you flexibility without sacrificing functionality.
